body.heading: One letter at a time
paragraphs: A word ladder starts with one word and ends with another, changing exactly one letter per step, with every in-between step a real word. CAT becomes DOG like this: CAT, COT, COG, DOG. Three small climbs, no jumps.

The game was invented by Lewis Carroll — the author of Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — who devised it in the 1870s and published it for readers of Vanity Fair. It survives because the rules fit in one sentence and the puzzles can still sting.

body.heading: A classic to try
paragraphs: Here is a famous one: turn COLD into WARM. Four steps will do it. The middle is the hard part — changing the first letter is easy, but every step must remain a word someone could use in a sentence.

Stuck? A good strategy is to work from both ends: find a word one step from COLD, and a word one step from WARM, and try to make the two lists meet in the middle. The answer is waiting in the takeaway.

body.heading: House rules for fair play
paragraphs: Agree the rules before you start: no proper names, no plurals made just by adding S (too easy), and every step must be a word you could look up. Some players allow four-letter words only; others climb from three letters to five by allowing a step that adds a letter.
Race a friend on the same ladder, or cooperate on one together. Either way, keep a notebook of ladders you have solved — you will start seeing one-letter friendships between words everywhere.

takeaway: Change one letter, keep a real word, repeat: CAT, COT, COG, DOG — and COLD reaches WARM in four steps: CORD, CARD, WARD, WARM.
